20-must-know-networking-concepts.title: Concepts 1–4: host, interface, MAC address, IP address
20-must-know-networking-concepts.body: A host is an endpoint that runs networked software. An interface is its attachment to a network, physical or virtual; one host can have several. A MAC address identifies an interface for delivery on many local links. An IP address identifies an interface or logical endpoint for IP routing. These identities have different scopes: changing Wi-Fi networks can change an IP address without changing the application running on the host.

20-must-know-networking-concepts.title: Concepts 5–8: subnet, gateway, switch, router
20-must-know-networking-concepts.body: A subnet describes an IP prefix whose membership affects routing decisions. A default gateway is a next-hop router used when a more specific route does not apply. A switch commonly forwards Ethernet frames within a link-layer domain. A router forwards IP packets between networks. For a remote destination, the first frame goes toward the gateway, while the packet still names the remote IP destination unless translation intervenes.

20-must-know-networking-concepts.title: Concepts 9–12: port, socket, packet, frame
20-must-know-networking-concepts.body: A port is a transport-layer number used to distinguish endpoint services. A socket is an operating-system communication object with protocol-specific state and addressing. An IP packet carries network-layer information and payload. A frame is a local-link transmission unit that can carry that packet. TCP port 443 is not a physical connector, and a socket is not itself a packet; confusing objects, identifiers, and transmitted units makes traces difficult to interpret.

20-must-know-networking-concepts.title: Concepts 13–16: DNS, DHCP, TCP, UDP
20-must-know-networking-concepts.body: DNS answers naming questions using typed records. DHCP can lease host configuration such as an IPv4 address, prefix information, routers, and resolvers. TCP supplies an ordered byte stream with reliability and congestion control. UDP supplies datagrams without those TCP guarantees. DNS and DHCP are application protocols using underlying transports; they are not replacements for IP. A resolver can be reachable while returning an incorrect or unavailable name.

20-must-know-networking-concepts.title: Concepts 17–20: HTTP, TLS, latency, bandwidth
20-must-know-networking-concepts.body: HTTP defines requests, responses, methods, metadata, and representation semantics. TLS protects a channel and authenticates peers according to its mode and validation policy. Latency measures delay, while bandwidth describes transmission capacity. Downloading a large object can benefit from more bandwidth; ten sequential remote requests still pay their dependency delays. HTTPS combines HTTP with security and transport choices, so measuring only one component cannot explain every website failure.

what-happens-when-you-type-a-url.title: URL interpretation and browser policy
what-happens-when-you-type-a-url.body: For https://shop.example:443/items?id=7#details, the scheme selects HTTPS, the hostname identifies the authority, the explicit port selects the endpoint, and the path plus query identify the requested target. The fragment is handled by the client and is not sent as part of the HTTP request target. Browser security policies, service workers, cached redirects, and stored transport policy can alter the subsequent work before any packet leaves.

what-happens-when-you-type-a-url.title: Name resolution and endpoint selection
what-happens-when-you-type-a-url.body: The browser and operating system may reuse cached DNS data; otherwise a resolver obtains suitable records. A and AAAA answers can provide multiple IPv4 and IPv6 candidates. Selecting and connecting to an address is separate from resolving it. A hostname may identify a CDN edge rather than the origin application. Record lookup timing, selected address family, and actual connected endpoint when reproducing a slow first visit.

what-happens-when-you-type-a-url.title: Transport, security, and request delivery
what-happens-when-you-type-a-url.body: With ordinary HTTP/2 over TLS over TCP, a new connection establishes TCP before completing the required TLS exchange, then sends HTTP frames. A reused connection skips much of that setup. HTTP/3 instead uses QUIC, whose security and transport establishment differ. The server may be a reverse proxy that creates another upstream connection. Therefore a single browser request can cross several distinct connections with separate timers and failures.

what-happens-when-you-type-a-url.title: Response processing and the rendering dependency graph
what-happens-when-you-type-a-url.body: HTML parsing discovers stylesheets, scripts, fonts, and images. These resources can create further requests, and script execution can delay parsing or introduce new work. Layout and painting consume CPU after network bytes arrive. A waterfall identifies dependencies: a script fetched quickly may still block useful rendering during execution. Compare first-byte time, resource completion, main-thread work, and visible rendering instead of treating response arrival as page completion.

packet-structure-and-encapsulation.title: Payload at one layer becomes data at the next
packet-structure-and-encapsulation.body: Suppose an application produces a message. TCP treats those bytes as a stream and adds transport information to segments; IP wraps a segment in a packet; Ethernet carries the packet in a frame. Ethernet also has a trailer for error detection. At reception, each implementation validates and interprets its own wrapper before delivering the relevant payload upward. These boundaries do not imply that one application message occupies exactly one segment.

packet-structure-and-encapsulation.title: Segmentation, fragmentation, and reassembly
packet-structure-and-encapsulation.body: TCP segmentation chooses portions of the byte stream for transmission. IP fragmentation divides an IP packet under version-specific rules, while application framing identifies messages within data. Losing a fragment prevents reconstruction of the original packet; TCP can recover lost stream bytes through retransmission. IPv6 routers do not fragment packets in transit. Applications sending large UDP datagrams therefore need particular care about path size limits and error handling.

packet-structure-and-encapsulation.title: A concrete header budget
packet-structure-and-encapsulation.body: Consider 1,000 bytes of TCP payload, a 20-byte TCP header, and a 20-byte IPv4 header without options. The IP packet is 1,040 bytes. An ordinary untagged Ethernet frame adds 14 header bytes and 4 FCS bytes, yielding 1,058 bytes from destination address through FCS. Preamble, start delimiter, and inter-frame gap consume additional link time. Tunnels and tags change this budget, so specify which measurement boundary a size includes.

packet-structure-and-encapsulation.title: What changes at a router
packet-structure-and-encapsulation.body: A router receives and checks incoming link framing, removes it, examines the IP destination, and selects an outgoing route. It reduces IPv4 TTL or IPv6 hop limit and applies relevant checks and policies. It then constructs outgoing link framing for the next hop. End-to-end transport data is normally preserved, but NAT, proxies, tunnels, and policy devices introduce additional transformations. Comparing captures requires accounting for the observation point.

network-types-lan-wan-vpn.title: LAN boundaries and broadcast domains
network-types-lan-wan-vpn.body: A LAN describes local connectivity and administration, but one building can contain several routed subnets and VLANs. A broadcast domain is the set of interfaces reached by a relevant link-layer broadcast. A router normally separates such domains. Wireless and wired clients can share one logical LAN through bridging, while neighboring desks can occupy isolated networks. Physical proximity therefore does not establish addressing scope or mutual access.

network-types-lan-wan-vpn.title: WAN links and the Internet
network-types-lan-wan-vpn.body: A WAN connects geographically separated sites through infrastructure such as provider circuits or routed overlays. The Internet is a federation of independently administered networks exchanging reachability. A WAN can be private, and Internet access can be one service carried over it. Distance, provider policy, bottleneck capacity, and return paths affect behavior; merely labeling a link WAN does not determine its latency, encryption, or reliability.

network-types-lan-wan-vpn.title: Remote-access and site-to-site VPNs
network-types-lan-wan-vpn.body: A remote-access VPN connects an endpoint into an overlay; a site-to-site VPN connects network regions through gateways. A full tunnel sends broadly selected traffic through the VPN, whereas split tunneling sends selected prefixes or destinations. Both require correct route selection, name resolution, keys, and access policy. Overlapping private address ranges can make a destination ambiguous even when the tunnel cryptography and handshake are working.

network-types-lan-wan-vpn.title: Choosing a topology with a failure example
network-types-lan-wan-vpn.body: Two offices using the same private /24 cannot be joined transparently by simply advertising both prefixes through a routed VPN. Renumbering, translation, or deliberately separated routing contexts may be necessary. Document endpoint addresses, gateways, prefixes, DNS views, and intended trust boundaries before connecting sites. Then test loss of a tunnel gateway and loss of the underlying access link separately, because their recovery mechanisms can differ.

ethernet-and-frames.title: Frame fields and minimum transmission size
ethernet-and-frames.body: An Ethernet II frame contains destination and source MAC addresses, an EtherType identifying the carried protocol, payload with padding where necessary, and an FCS. The ordinary untagged frame minimum is 64 bytes from destination address through FCS; the familiar 1,500-byte MTU describes the usual payload limit, not the total frame on the medium. VLAN tags and larger supported MTUs require explicit accounting.

ethernet-and-frames.title: Learning and forwarding decisions
ethernet-and-frames.body: A learning switch associates the source MAC of an incoming frame with its ingress port within the relevant VLAN. A known unicast destination can be forwarded toward a learned port. Unknown unicast and broadcast forwarding generally replicate within the allowed domain, excluding the ingress port and respecting policy. Entries age so moved or disconnected devices do not leave permanent mappings. Learning observes sources; it does not authenticate ownership.

ethernet-and-frames.title: Loops and spanning trees
ethernet-and-frames.body: A physical loop between bridges can circulate broadcasts and unknown unicasts, creating repeated traffic and unstable MAC learning. Ethernet frames do not carry an IP-style hop limit to solve this. Spanning-tree mechanisms select a loop-free active topology, while other designs use explicitly controlled alternatives. Redundant links need a loop-prevention or aggregation design; adding a cable for resilience without one can take down an otherwise healthy LAN.

ethernet-and-frames.title: Collision history versus modern full duplex
ethernet-and-frames.body: Shared half-duplex Ethernet used collision detection and backoff because several transmitters could contend for one medium. Modern switched full-duplex links provide separate transmit and receive directions and do not use that shared collision mechanism in normal operation. Wi-Fi contention follows different rules. When diagnosing errors, distinguish physical corruption, duplex misconfiguration, queue drops, and switching loops instead of describing every lost frame as a collision.

mac-vs-ip-addresses.title: Local delivery versus routed reachability
mac-vs-ip-addresses.body: An Ethernet destination MAC selects delivery on the current link, while an IP destination directs routed forwarding across networks. A packet for 203.0.113.8 can leave a laptop in a frame addressed to its gateway's MAC. At the next routed link, that frame is replaced. The destination IP can remain 203.0.113.8 across the path, although NAT or proxying can deliberately alter what particular observers see.

mac-vs-ip-addresses.title: Addresses are scoped and replaceable
mac-vs-ip-addresses.body: An interface may use a factory-assigned or locally administered MAC address, including randomized addresses. IP addresses may be statically configured, leased, temporary, or one of several assigned to an interface. Neither identifier is an enduring person identity. A host with Ethernet, Wi-Fi, and a VPN can expose several simultaneous addresses and routes. Troubleshooting must identify which interface and source address the operating system actually selected.

mac-vs-ip-addresses.title: Neighbor resolution follows route selection
mac-vs-ip-addresses.body: First determine whether the destination is on-link or requires a gateway using the routing table. Then resolve the local next-hop address using ARP for IPv4 Ethernet or neighbor discovery for IPv6. An off-link destination ordinarily causes resolution of the router, not of the distant server. A cached neighbor mapping can make successful communication possible without an ARP request appearing in a short packet capture.

mac-vs-ip-addresses.title: A practical identity comparison
mac-vs-ip-addresses.body: A DNS name identifies a naming entry, an IP address selects network reachability, a port selects a transport endpoint, and an authenticated certificate can bind a service identity to a key. These solve different problems. If an attacker advertises a misleading local address mapping, packets may be redirected without changing the URL. Correct higher-layer authentication can still reject the impersonating peer, demonstrating why address reachability alone is insufficient trust.

switches-hubs-routers.title: Hub: repeat the physical signal
switches-hubs-routers.body: A hub operates as a shared-medium repeater and does not choose an output using a destination MAC table. Participants share collision behavior on traditional half-duplex Ethernet and receive repeated signaling. Adding hosts increases contention rather than creating independent switched paths. This historical device is useful for understanding why physical repetition and intelligent forwarding are separate functions; modern Ethernet networks generally use switches instead.

switches-hubs-routers.title: Switch: learn local destinations
switches-hubs-routers.body: A Layer-2 switch learns source locations and forwards frames within VLAN policy. Each switched port can form an independent full-duplex link, while broadcasts still span the relevant VLAN. A switch may also offer VLAN tagging, link aggregation, spanning tree, and security controls. Its forwarding database is different from an IP routing table: a MAC entry identifies a local forwarding location, not a route to a remote IP prefix.

switches-hubs-routers.title: Router: select an IP next hop
switches-hubs-routers.body: A router compares the destination IP against routes, chooses the most specific matching prefix, and sends the packet over the selected next hop or interface. It separates ordinary Layer-2 broadcast domains and can enforce policies across them. Routers participate in ARP or neighbor discovery on their attached links. A router need not know every host MAC on the Internet; it needs the neighbor appropriate to each outgoing local link.

switches-hubs-routers.title: Combined devices and a forwarding exercise
switches-hubs-routers.body: A home Wi-Fi router commonly includes an access point, Ethernet switch, IP router, NAT, DHCP service, and firewall. A product label therefore conceals several mechanisms. Draw two local clients and one remote server: client-to-client traffic may be bridged, while server-bound traffic is routed and possibly translated. Diagnose the function involved in the failing path rather than assuming restarting the entire combined device identifies the cause.

arp-protocol.title: Request and reply sequence
arp-protocol.body: On an IPv4 Ethernet link, a sender missing a neighbor mapping broadcasts an ARP request identifying the target IPv4 address. The matching neighbor normally replies with its link address, allowing the sender to construct an Ethernet frame. The request and reply carry sender and target protocol and hardware information. ARP is carried directly by the local link and is not forwarded as an IP packet by ordinary routers.

arp-protocol.title: The cache has a lifecycle
arp-protocol.body: Neighbor information is cached to avoid resolving every packet independently. Entries can become stale, be refreshed, fail verification, or be replaced under implementation-specific behavior. If a gateway changes hardware, cached mappings may briefly direct traffic incorrectly. Distinguish a missing route from a failed neighbor entry: the former cannot select a path, while the latter cannot deliver to the selected next hop on its local link.

arp-protocol.title: Gratuitous ARP, probes, and proxy ARP
arp-protocol.body: A device can announce its own mapping or probe whether an address is already in use. These patterns support address-conflict detection and failover, but their purposes differ from a normal request for a remote neighbor. With proxy ARP, a router answers on behalf of another address and accepts the associated traffic. Such behavior can hide topology from hosts and must be diagnosed against deliberate configuration.

arp-protocol.title: Spoofing and the IPv6 distinction
arp-protocol.body: ARP does not inherently authenticate the claimed IP-to-MAC binding, so an attacker on an applicable local network may try to poison neighbor state. Switch controls, segmentation, and endpoint authentication provide different defenses. IPv6 uses neighbor discovery over ICMPv6 rather than ARP; filtering all ICMPv6 can therefore break essential local operation. Learn the resolution mechanism for the active address family before selecting diagnostic commands.

vlans-and-segmentation.title: Access ports and tagged trunks
vlans-and-segmentation.body: An access port commonly places untagged endpoint traffic into a configured VLAN. A trunk can carry multiple VLANs, usually distinguishing them with IEEE 802.1Q tags. Each VLAN represents a separate logical Layer-2 domain under the switch configuration. Native or untagged handling is configuration-sensitive, so mismatches can move traffic into unintended domains. Record both endpoint membership and trunk allowed-VLAN policy when following a path.

vlans-and-segmentation.title: Inter-VLAN routing is a separate operation
vlans-and-segmentation.body: Hosts in different VLANs normally need Layer-3 forwarding to communicate. A router or Layer-3 switch can provide a gateway interface for each subnet and apply policy between them. Assigning two VLAN identifiers does not itself define who may communicate after routing. For guest and employee networks, inspect the routed firewall rules as well as the switching separation; otherwise both may still reach the same sensitive service.

vlans-and-segmentation.title: VLANs, subnets, and broadcast traffic
vlans-and-segmentation.body: A common design pairs a VLAN with an IP subnet, but VLAN membership and IP addressing are distinct configurations. A host placed in the wrong VLAN can retain a plausible static address while failing to reach its gateway. Broadcasts and ARP remain within the configured link domain unless a special relay or forwarding feature intervenes. DHCP relays can deliberately connect local clients with a server elsewhere.

vlans-and-segmentation.title: A complete isolation test
vlans-and-segmentation.body: Put two test endpoints in the intended VLANs and verify local addressing, gateway reachability, allowed application paths, and denied application paths. Inspect tags at a suitable trunk observation point and remember that a host capture can omit tags because of offload. Test a wrongly connected port and a missing trunk allowance. An isolation design is verified by attempted prohibited communication, not merely by seeing different VLAN numbers in a dashboard.

wifi-802-11-basics.title: Stations, access points, and association
wifi-802-11-basics.body: A station joins a basic service set through an access point after relevant discovery, authentication, and association exchanges. The visible network name is an SSID; it is not a unique proof of a trusted physical device. Multiple access points can advertise the same SSID. Joining the wireless link is distinct from acquiring IP configuration, resolving names, or passing a captive portal, so diagnose those stages separately.

wifi-802-11-basics.title: Shared airtime and contention
wifi-802-11-basics.body: Wi-Fi stations contend for airtime using carrier-sense and backoff mechanisms rather than Ethernet's old collision-detection model. Interference, hidden transmitters, retries, and low-rate clients consume shared channel time. A client reporting a high physical link rate does not receive that rate as sustained application throughput. Protocol overhead and other users share the medium, and contention can increase latency even when signal strength looks good.

wifi-802-11-basics.title: Channels, bands, and roaming
wifi-802-11-basics.body: Channel width, frequency band, neighboring transmitters, walls, and antenna placement influence usable capacity and interference. Wider channels can increase peak rates while reducing opportunities for non-overlapping reuse. During roaming, a station changes association and may incur authentication or path-update delays. A stable SSID does not guarantee uninterrupted transport. Test movement and loaded-channel behavior, not only a stationary speed test beside one access point.

wifi-802-11-basics.title: Security and a diagnostic comparison
wifi-802-11-basics.body: Wireless authentication and encryption protect the local radio association under the selected security mode. They do not replace HTTPS identity verification, application authorization, or protection beyond the access point. Compare the same workload over wired and wireless links, then examine retries, channel occupancy, and signal quality. If only Wi-Fi degrades under competing clients, focus on airtime and interference before changing a server's TCP configuration.

ipv4-addressing.title: Thirty-two bits and prefix membership
ipv4-addressing.body: An IPv4 address has 32 bits, conventionally written as four decimal octets. A prefix length specifies how many leading bits identify a route or subnet. For 192.168.10.77/26, the mask is 255.255.255.192 and the block spans .64 through .127. The address itself does not encode which host role is a gateway; that comes from route configuration. Classful A/B/C rules are historical rather than the basis of modern CIDR routing.

ipv4-addressing.title: Public, private, loopback, and link-local uses
ipv4-addressing.body: Private IPv4 ranges support internal addressing and are not globally unique across organizations. Loopback addresses refer to the local host, while link-local addressing serves a different limited scope. Documentation ranges are intended for examples. Address scope affects where routing is meaningful, but private does not mean encrypted or authorized. Joining two independently configured private networks can expose overlapping prefixes and ambiguous destinations.

ipv4-addressing.title: Network and broadcast conventions
ipv4-addressing.body: For an ordinary IPv4 multi-access subnet, the all-zero host portion identifies the network and the all-one host portion identifies its directed broadcast address. Traditional usable-host arithmetic subtracts those two addresses. A /31 point-to-point link and a /32 host route are important exceptions. Do not mechanically apply subtract-two arithmetic to every prefix, and distinguish a subnet-directed broadcast from the limited broadcast used on the local network.

ipv4-addressing.title: Exhaustion and operational consequences
ipv4-addressing.body: The 32-bit address space cannot supply unrestricted globally unique addresses to every modern endpoint. Allocation practices, address reuse through NAT, and IPv6 deployment address different parts of this constraint. NAT introduces state and inbound-connectivity complications rather than creating more globally unique IPv4 bits. When planning capacity, distinguish endpoint count, public address count, simultaneous translation ports, and failure behavior of the translation device.

ipv6.title: Address notation and scopes
ipv6.body: IPv6 addresses have 128 bits written as hexadecimal groups. Leading zeroes can be omitted within a group, and one consecutive run of zero groups can be compressed with a double colon. Global, link-local, loopback, and multicast addresses have different roles. A link-local destination may require an interface scope because the same address form can occur on multiple links. IPv6 does not use IPv4-style broadcast delivery.

ipv6.title: Base header and extension processing
ipv6.body: The IPv6 base header is fixed at 40 bytes and carries source and destination addresses, payload length, next-header information, hop limit, traffic class, and flow label. Optional information can be carried through extension headers. Routers reduce hop limit during forwarding and do not fragment packets in transit. A sender must account for path size constraints, with ICMPv6 Packet Too Big feedback playing an important role.

ipv6.title: Neighbor discovery and host configuration
ipv6.body: Neighbor discovery uses ICMPv6 for functions including neighbor address resolution and router discovery. Router advertisements can provide prefixes and other information, while SLAAC and DHCPv6 have different configuration roles. DHCPv6 does not simply replace all router-discovery behavior. Blocking required ICMPv6 can break address resolution or path-size handling even when a firewall rule permits the final application's TCP or UDP port.

ipv6.title: Dual-stack troubleshooting example
ipv6.body: A service publishes both A and AAAA records, but only its IPv4 listener is reachable. Some clients succeed through IPv4 while others first attempt the broken IPv6 path. Check the actual address family and selected endpoint rather than assuming one successful hostname request proves both paths. Verify listener bindings, routing, firewall rules, DNS, and return traffic separately for each family before removing the symptom by disabling IPv6.

subnetting-and-cidr.title: Binary masks and block alignment
subnetting-and-cidr.body: A /27 keeps 27 network bits and leaves five host bits, producing 32-address blocks. In a /24, their final-octet starts are 0, 32, 64, 96, 128, 160, 192, and 224. An address ending in 77 belongs to the block starting at 64. A valid network prefix must align on its block boundary; writing an arbitrary host address with /27 does not create a new overlapping block starting there.

subnetting-and-cidr.title: Variable-length subnet planning
subnetting-and-cidr.body: Suppose a /24 must serve ordinary LANs needing 100, 50, and 20 hosts. Allocate a /25 with 126 conventional host addresses, then a /26 with 62, then a /27 with 30, respecting boundaries. The remaining /27 can be reserved. Allocate larger requirements first to reduce fragmentation. Include growth, gateway addresses, reservations, and actual platform behavior rather than assigning a prefix from today's endpoint count alone.

subnetting-and-cidr.title: Aggregation and longest-prefix matching
subnetting-and-cidr.body: Adjacent aligned prefixes can sometimes be summarized: 10.0.0.0/24 and 10.0.1.0/24 fit 10.0.0.0/23. Summarizing unrelated ranges can announce reachability to addresses the router cannot serve. During lookup, a /24 matching a destination takes precedence over a matching /16, which takes precedence over a default /0. Route preference between competing routes of equal specificity is a separate policy question.

subnetting-and-cidr.title: Worked overlap check
subnetting-and-cidr.body: Two teams propose 192.168.4.0/25 and 192.168.4.64/26. The first spans .0 through .127, while the second spans .64 through .127, so the allocations overlap completely within that range. Compare interval boundaries or masked prefixes before deployment. Separate address-allocation validation from forwarding behavior: a router may intentionally carry overlapping routes, but assigning overlapping independent LAN ranges usually creates ambiguity that routing alone does not solve.

how-routing-works.title: Destination lookup and next-hop resolution
how-routing-works.body: A host or router performs a routing lookup for the destination under its applicable policy and routing context. The selected entry can specify an outgoing interface and next-hop gateway. If the next hop is on an Ethernet link, neighbor resolution obtains the address needed for the outgoing frame. A route can exist while that neighbor is unreachable, so routing-table success and forwarding success are distinct observations.

how-routing-works.title: Control plane and data plane
how-routing-works.body: The control plane learns or configures routes using static settings and routing protocols. The data plane forwards individual packets using installed forwarding information. A correct protocol advertisement does not prove the forwarding hardware or neighbor state is correct. Conversely, packets can continue using an installed route while a control-plane session is temporarily disrupted. Troubleshooting should compare learned routes, selected routes, installed forwarding entries, and actual traffic.

how-routing-works.title: Longest prefix and default route example
how-routing-works.body: Given routes for 10.0.0.0/8 through A, 10.2.0.0/16 through B, and 0.0.0.0/0 through C, destination 10.2.3.4 matches all three but uses the /16 route under ordinary longest-prefix forwarding. Destination 10.9.1.1 uses the /8 route, and 203.0.113.7 uses the default. Additional policy routing can select a different table, so include source-based or marked-traffic policy when the observed result differs.

how-routing-works.title: Loops, asymmetry, and convergence
how-routing-works.body: Routing changes can temporarily produce blackholes or loops while devices update at different times. TTL or hop limit bounds indefinite packet circulation but does not repair the underlying route. Return traffic can follow a different path, which matters to stateful firewalls and measurements. A traceroute in one direction is therefore incomplete evidence for a bidirectional application. Observe both directions and correlate failures with route-change timing.

bgp-and-ospf.title: OSPF builds an internal topology view
bgp-and-ospf.body: OSPF routers exchange link-state information, maintain a topology database within its area structure, and compute shortest paths using configured costs. Neighbor relationships and reliable distribution support consistent knowledge, while areas limit the scope of some information. The computed cost is an administrative metric rather than a direct live latency measurement. A failed adjacency, mismatched configuration, or missing advertisement can therefore prevent reachability even when a physical link is up.

bgp-and-ospf.title: BGP distributes reachability with policy
bgp-and-ospf.body: BGP advertises IP prefixes with attributes, including AS-path information, between peers. External BGP connects autonomous systems; internal BGP distributes relevant routing information within one system. Import and export policy determines which advertisements are accepted or propagated. Operators use attributes and local policy to choose routes, so the winning path need not have the fewest kilometers or lowest RTT. The session uses TCP, but routing correctness depends on the exchanged policy.

bgp-and-ospf.title: Path selection and route leaks
bgp-and-ospf.body: AS-path information helps identify loops across autonomous systems, while attributes such as local preference express operator choices. Route filtering and authorization matter because an unintended announcement can attract traffic to an unusable or unauthorized path. A more specific prefix may win forwarding even when an aggregate remains visible. Validate both the origin and permitted propagation scope of routes rather than treating every reachable BGP peer as a source of trustworthy advertisements.

bgp-and-ospf.title: Convergence exercise
bgp-and-ospf.body: When a link fails, detection precedes information distribution, route recomputation, and forwarding installation. Applications can see loss during any of those intervals. Compare an internal OSPF change with an external BGP withdrawal: their scope, policy, and propagation differ. Faster timers may reduce detection time while increasing sensitivity or load. Measure end-to-end recovery and packet forwarding, not merely the instant a routing daemon reports its new preferred path.

nat-and-pat.title: Address translation and port translation
nat-and-pat.body: Basic NAT translates address information, while port address translation also distinguishes transport flows through translated ports. A gateway can map 10.0.0.5:51000 and 10.0.0.6:51000 to different public-side source ports on one address. It must maintain enough state to translate matching return traffic. Translation changes observable endpoint tuples, so captures on the internal and external interfaces cannot be compared by an unchanged five-tuple alone.

nat-and-pat.title: Outbound mapping and inbound reachability
nat-and-pat.body: An outbound packet can create translation state that permits the corresponding response under the device's policy. An unrelated inbound connection lacks that association unless a static mapping, forwarding rule, or other mechanism handles it. NAT behavior and firewall permission are separate concepts even when one device supplies both. A successful outbound request therefore does not prove an external client can initiate a connection to the same internal host.

nat-and-pat.title: State lifetime and exhaustion
nat-and-pat.body: Translation mappings expire according to protocol and device policy. A quiet UDP application can discover that an old mapping no longer works, while large numbers of connections can exhaust available ports or state capacity. Keepalives consume traffic and are not a universal cure. Plan the number of simultaneously active destinations and flows, reuse behavior, idle lifetime, and failover state replication before sizing a heavily shared egress gateway.

nat-and-pat.title: Protocol complications and debugging
nat-and-pat.body: Protocols that embed addresses inside payloads may require special handling because rewriting outer headers does not update application data. Encryption can prevent intermediary payload rewriting entirely. Hairpin traffic, where an internal client uses an external mapping for another internal service, depends on gateway support. During diagnosis, record pre- and post-translation tuples and timestamps, then check return routes and state expiry before concluding the destination server dropped the request.

icmp-ping-traceroute.title: ICMP carries control information
icmp-ping-traceroute.body: ICMP reports selected network conditions and supports diagnostic exchanges; it is not a transport replacement for TCP or UDP. Echo request and reply underpin common ping use, while unreachable and time-exceeded messages explain certain forwarding failures. Some errors quote portions of the packet that caused them. Devices can filter or rate-limit these messages, so their absence is ambiguous and their presence must be interpreted by type and code.

icmp-ping-traceroute.title: Ping measures a particular round trip
icmp-ping-traceroute.body: A ping sends an echo request and measures time until a matching reply, optionally reporting unanswered probes. Its RTT includes forward and return paths plus endpoint processing. Successful echo does not establish that HTTPS is permitted, that DNS resolves correctly, or that the application is healthy. Conversely, blocked echo can coexist with a working website. Compare the diagnostic exchange with the actual failing application's path and protocol.

icmp-ping-traceroute.title: Traceroute uses deliberately limited lifetimes
icmp-ping-traceroute.body: Traceroute sends probes with increasing TTL or hop limit. Routers where that value expires may report time exceeded, revealing a responding interface and round-trip timing to that point. Implementations use different probe transports. Asterisks mean no usable reply arrived for those probes; they do not necessarily mark a forwarding outage. Load balancing and asymmetric return paths can make the output differ across probes and directions.

icmp-ping-traceroute.title: Path MTU and a large-packet failure
icmp-ping-traceroute.body: An IPv4 packet marked do-not-fragment may trigger a fragmentation-needed error when too large for an outgoing link; IPv6 relies on Packet Too Big information because routers do not fragment in transit. If essential feedback is lost, small exchanges can succeed while larger transfers stall. Investigate tunnel overhead and effective path MTU. Permit required control messages according to policy rather than treating every ICMP message as optional diagnostic noise.

dhcp.title: Discover: locate a configuration service
dhcp.body: A newly configuring DHCPv4 client can broadcast DHCPDISCOVER because it does not yet have a usable leased address or know a server. The exchange carries information allowing replies to be associated with that client and transaction. DHCP uses UDP, conventionally client port 68 and server port 67. A relay can carry the local discovery toward a server on another subnet, so the server need not share the client's broadcast domain.

dhcp.title: Offer and Request: propose and select a lease
dhcp.body: A server responds with DHCPOFFER containing a proposed address and configuration. More than one server can offer. The client selects an offer and sends DHCPREQUEST to identify its selection and requested configuration; in the initial selection exchange this informs the other participating servers as well. Receiving an offer alone does not mean the client has completed lease acquisition. Capture all messages before concluding configuration succeeded.

dhcp.title: Acknowledge: commit the usable configuration
dhcp.body: The selected server returns DHCPACK when it grants the request, including the lease and relevant options. A client then performs the applicable configuration and conflict checks before normal use. DHCPNAK instead rejects an invalid request under the protocol's rules. The familiar initial sequence is Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge—four distinct messages. A missing ACK, invalid options, or address conflict can leave a client unable to communicate despite having seen an offer.

dhcp.title: Renewal, rebinding, release, and expiry
dhcp.body: A lease has a finite lifetime. A bound client first attempts renewal with its server and later can rebind through other available servers if renewal fails, according to supplied or default timers. Successful renewal need not repeat the original four-message discovery path. If the lease expires without renewal, the client must stop using it as permitted by the protocol. Release, decline after conflict, pool exhaustion, and relay configuration are separate diagnostic cases.

tcp-vs-udp.title: Delivery contract and message boundaries
tcp-vs-udp.body: TCP presents bytes in order and suppresses duplicate delivery within its stream abstraction; it does not preserve the boundaries of application writes. UDP delivers separate datagrams and does not itself restore lost ones or reorder them into an application stream. A 100-byte TCP write might require several reads, whereas a UDP receiver handles one datagram at a time subject to buffer and API rules. Choose application framing accordingly.

tcp-vs-udp.title: Connection state, flow control, and congestion
tcp-vs-udp.body: TCP maintains connection state, acknowledges bytes, advertises receiver capacity, and regulates offered traffic using congestion control. UDP's smaller base contract leaves those responsibilities to the application or a protocol built above it when needed. Absence of a TCP handshake does not mean unlimited safe sending. A UDP-based file transfer still needs rate control, integrity, loss handling, and receiver-resource limits if it is to behave responsibly on shared networks.

tcp-vs-udp.title: Selecting a transport by semantics
tcp-vs-udp.body: A financial request needs a clear application outcome and duplicate protection regardless of transport. A live media application may prefer a recent frame to retransmission of an obsolete frame, but still needs congestion control and loss tolerance. QUIC demonstrates that a protocol can use UDP as its carrier while providing reliable streams. Compare latency deadlines, ordering requirements, message size, network reachability, and implementation cost instead of equating UDP with automatically faster applications.

tcp-vs-udp.title: Failure observations are not business outcomes
tcp-vs-udp.body: A successful local send means the operating system accepted data under that API, not that a remote application committed an operation. A TCP acknowledgment concerns transport reception, while an application response can convey a stronger result. A connection reset or timeout can occur after server-side work completed. For retryable operations, design identifiers and result recovery around this ambiguity instead of relying on the apparent reliability of the selected transport.

tcp-three-way-handshake.title: First message: SYN establishes the client's sequence proposal
tcp-three-way-handshake.body: In ordinary active establishment, the client sends a segment with SYN and its initial sequence number, then waits in SYN-SENT. SYN consumes one sequence number even when it carries no application payload. Options can advertise capabilities such as maximum segment size, window scaling, timestamps, and selective acknowledgment support. Those capabilities are negotiated per connection; a later capture that missed setup may lack context needed to interpret subsequent fields.

tcp-three-way-handshake.title: Second message: SYN-ACK acknowledges and proposes
tcp-three-way-handshake.body: A listening server receiving an acceptable SYN creates the appropriate pending state and normally responds with SYN plus ACK. Its acknowledgment is the client's initial sequence number plus one, and its own sequence number begins the reverse direction. For client initial 1,000 and server initial 9,000, this response uses sequence 9,000 and acknowledgment 1,001. Each direction therefore has an independent sequence space, rather than sharing one packet counter.

tcp-three-way-handshake.title: Third message: ACK completes ordinary establishment
tcp-three-way-handshake.body: The client acknowledges the server's SYN using acknowledgment 9,001 in the example, while its own next sequence is 1,001. The server can then complete the transition to ESTABLISHED under the normal path. The acknowledgment confirms receipt of the server's sequence proposal; it is not a user authentication step. TCP establishment alone says nothing about TLS identity, HTTP authorization, database readiness, or whether an application will accept the request.

tcp-three-way-handshake.title: Loss, simultaneous open, and queue boundaries
tcp-three-way-handshake.body: Handshake messages can be lost and retransmitted, adding delay without proving the service is down. A lost final acknowledgment may be resolved by later valid traffic or retransmission behavior. Simultaneous open is a different valid state path from the ordinary client/listener diagram. Pending handshake state and established connections waiting for application acceptance are distinct resources. A SYN flood and a server that stops accepting connections stress different parts of establishment.

tcp-connection-termination.title: The ordinary active-close path
tcp-connection-termination.body: An endpoint that has finished sending transmits FIN and normally moves from ESTABLISHED to FIN-WAIT-1. Once its FIN is acknowledged it enters FIN-WAIT-2, waiting for the other direction to finish. FIN consumes one sequence number. The peer may acknowledge immediately while continuing to send its own remaining data. Closing is consequently not the same as a single message that erases both directions at once.

tcp-connection-termination.title: Passive close and the final acknowledgment
tcp-connection-termination.body: The peer receiving FIN acknowledges it and enters CLOSE-WAIT while its application decides when to close its sending direction. After sending its own FIN it waits in LAST-ACK. The active closer acknowledges that FIN and enters TIME-WAIT in the ordinary path. FIN and ACK can be combined, so a correct close is not required to appear as exactly four separate packets in every trace.

tcp-connection-termination.title: Complete state vocabulary and alternate paths
tcp-connection-termination.body: The classic TCP states are CLOSED, LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSE-WAIT, CLOSING, LAST-ACK, and TIME-WAIT. Simultaneous close can involve CLOSING instead of the ordinary passive-close sequence. A reset aborts an applicable connection rather than following graceful FIN exchange. These states describe protocol progress, not whether application data has been durably stored or a business transaction has succeeded.

tcp-connection-termination.title: Diagnosing CLOSE-WAIT and TIME-WAIT
tcp-connection-termination.body: Persistent CLOSE-WAIT often means the peer finished sending but the local application has not closed its side; inspect ownership and cleanup paths. TIME-WAIT protects against delayed segments and supports handling retransmitted closing traffic. Its count is influenced by connection churn and which endpoint actively closes. Do not treat both states as equivalent leaks or blindly shorten timers. Compare connection lifetimes, open descriptors, and application completion behavior first.

tcp-header-anatomy.title: Ports, sequence numbers, and acknowledgment numbers
tcp-header-anatomy.body: Source and destination ports are 16-bit transport identifiers. The 32-bit sequence number identifies the position of segment data within one direction's byte stream, and the 32-bit acknowledgment number normally reports the next expected byte when ACK is set. An acknowledgment of 5,501 cumulatively covers preceding contiguous sequence space, not 5,501 packets. SYN and FIN also occupy sequence space, which matters when doing arithmetic around connection setup and close.

tcp-header-anatomy.title: Data offset, receive window, checksum, urgent pointer
tcp-header-anatomy.body: Data offset expresses the TCP header length in 32-bit words and therefore separates options from payload. The advertised window communicates receiver-side capacity, interpreted with negotiated scaling where applicable. The checksum covers TCP information plus a pseudo-header tied to the IP endpoints; it is error detection rather than authentication. The urgent pointer has meaning when URG is set and should not be confused with a general priority or low-latency guarantee.

tcp-header-anatomy.title: Control flags and their distinct meanings
tcp-header-anatomy.body: SYN synchronizes sequence spaces, FIN ends one direction, RST resets an applicable connection, and ACK makes the acknowledgment field significant. PSH requests prompt delivery under TCP's push semantics; it does not preserve application message boundaries. URG marks urgent-pointer significance. ECE and CWR support explicit congestion notification behavior. Interpret flags together with state and sequence validity; a flag bit by itself does not establish a complete explanation of a captured exchange.

tcp-header-anatomy.title: Options and a header-size calculation
tcp-header-anatomy.body: A TCP header without options is 20 bytes. Maximum segment size, window scale, selective-acknowledgment negotiation or blocks, and timestamps are examples of options with their own formats and rules. Data offset includes padding needed for alignment. If an IPv4 packet has a 20-byte IP header and a 32-byte TCP header inside a 1,500-byte IP MTU, at most 1,448 bytes remain for TCP payload in that packet, before any additional encapsulation.

reliability-acks-retransmission.title: Cumulative acknowledgment and missing ranges
reliability-acks-retransmission.body: Suppose bytes 1–1,000 and 2,001–3,000 arrive, but 1,001–2,000 do not. The receiver cannot advance cumulative acknowledgment beyond the missing range, even though it can buffer later bytes. After the gap arrives, cumulative progress can cover the whole contiguous range. Selective acknowledgment can additionally describe ranges already received, allowing the sender to avoid unnecessarily retransmitting every byte after the first gap.

reliability-acks-retransmission.title: Timers and ambiguous RTT measurements
reliability-acks-retransmission.body: Retransmission timers must account for observed round-trip time and its variability. A timer that is too short produces unnecessary duplicates; one that is too long delays recovery. Acknowledgments following retransmission can make it unclear which transmission they acknowledge unless supporting mechanisms resolve the ambiguity. Real implementations therefore use defined estimation and backoff rules rather than a universal fixed timeout that suits every path and workload.

reliability-acks-retransmission.title: Fast recovery signals versus timeout recovery
reliability-acks-retransmission.body: Repeated acknowledgment information and selective ranges can indicate that later data arrived while a gap remains, enabling loss recovery before a full retransmission timeout. Reordering can produce similar observations, so loss detection requires careful rules. Timeout recovery is a separate event and can cause stronger reduction of sending behavior. Read a trace as ranges, acknowledgments, and timing evidence rather than labeling every duplicate ACK as definitive proof of one specific loss.

reliability-acks-retransmission.title: Reliability stops at the transport boundary
reliability-acks-retransmission.body: TCP can deliver request bytes exactly once within its stream abstraction while an application executes the same logical operation twice across retried connections. Conversely, a server may acknowledge bytes before its process reads or persists them. Sequence numbers are not transaction identifiers. If a reply is lost after a purchase commits, the client needs an application operation key or status query to resolve the result safely.

flow-control-sliding-window.title: A moving interval of permitted byte positions
flow-control-sliding-window.body: The receive window describes an interval of sequence space relative to the acknowledged position, rather than a permanent fixed number of packets. As the application consumes data, the receiver can advertise more capacity and the interval advances. Segments have different payload lengths, so reasoning in bytes avoids mistakes. The sender must combine this receiver limit with its own congestion and recovery constraints before releasing additional stream data.

flow-control-sliding-window.title: Window scaling and high-bandwidth paths
flow-control-sliding-window.body: The base TCP window field is 16 bits. Window scaling negotiated during setup allows representation of larger receive windows, helping paths that require substantial data in flight. A packet capture without the handshake can misinterpret a scaled window. Scaling expands the representation; it does not allocate unlimited memory or guarantee throughput. The application still needs to drain data, and congestion control can remain the smaller active limit.

flow-control-sliding-window.title: Zero-window behavior and the persist problem
flow-control-sliding-window.body: If the receiving application stops consuming data, the receiver can advertise a zero window. The sender must respect the lack of space while still handling recovery of window information under TCP's mechanisms. If a later window-opening update is lost, the connection should not remain stuck forever merely because both sides are waiting. This is why zero-window handling is a distinct protocol concern from ordinary packet-loss congestion recovery.

flow-control-sliding-window.title: A complete allowance calculation
flow-control-sliding-window.body: Assume a receive limit of 96 KiB, a congestion limit of 64 KiB, and 48 KiB outstanding. The simplified permitted new-data volume is min(96, 64) minus 48, or 16 KiB. If the receiver reduces its limit to 32 KiB while 48 KiB is already outstanding, the new-data allowance becomes zero rather than negative transmission. Already sent bytes do not disappear; sending waits for conditions that permit further progress.

congestion-control.title: Slow start and the threshold
congestion-control.body: Slow start rapidly grows the congestion window while acknowledgments report progress, often approximated as doubling per round trip under ideal assumptions. It ends when the algorithm reaches a threshold or responds to congestion. This growth concerns outstanding data, not a promise that physical bandwidth doubles. Delayed acknowledgments, application-limited sending, pacing, losses, and implementation rules make a real trace more complex than a simple 1, 2, 4, 8 diagram.

congestion-control.title: AIMD and Reno congestion avoidance
congestion-control.body: Additive increase probes more cautiously while multiplicative decrease retreats after congestion. Reno is a useful reference for this family: in an idealized congestion-avoidance model the window grows roughly one maximum-sized segment per RTT, and a loss response reduces its operating window. Fast retransmit and recovery differ from timeout handling. State which loss signal and recovery stage are being modeled before claiming every loss always halves the current sending rate.

congestion-control.title: CUBIC's time-based growth
congestion-control.body: CUBIC uses a cubic function of elapsed time around a remembered congestion point, allowing growth to behave differently from Reno's linear increase. It can probe beyond a previous operating point while treating the region near it more cautiously. Its behavior is not simply constant exponential growth. Compare fairness, recovery, RTT sensitivity, and queueing under representative competing flows; a single isolated transfer cannot establish how a controller shares a bottleneck.

congestion-control.title: BBR's delivery-rate and delay model
congestion-control.body: BBR estimates bottleneck delivery rate and propagation-related round-trip time, then uses a model to guide pacing and data in flight. It is not merely a loss-triggered variant of Reno. Measurement can be affected by application-limited sending, changing paths, and competing traffic, and BBR versions differ. Evaluating it requires more than a peak-throughput number: observe latency, loss, coexistence, and whether the test reaches a steady operating regime.

congestion-control.title: ECN, pacing, and bottleneck queues
congestion-control.body: Explicit Congestion Notification permits supporting network elements and endpoints to signal congestion without relying only on dropped packets. Pacing spreads transmission over time, while a window bounds outstanding volume; either alone does not describe the whole sending pattern. A deep queue can maintain high throughput while causing severe delay, often called bufferbloat. Include queueing latency and responsiveness in performance goals instead of maximizing only the number of bytes acknowledged.

congestion-control.title: Worked comparison with explicit assumptions
congestion-control.body: Take an idealized initial window of four segments and a threshold of sixteen. Slow-start rounds might allow 4, 8, and 16 segments; Reno-like congestion avoidance can then grow to 17 and 18. This is a teaching model with continuous data and simplified acknowledgment behavior. Change RTT from 20 to 100 ms and the same number of growth rounds takes five times longer, explaining why startup can dominate short transfers.

head-of-line-blocking.title: Queue order can create artificial dependency
head-of-line-blocking.body: Head-of-line blocking occurs when the first pending item prevents later useful work from progressing even if that later work could otherwise be served. It appears in network queues, application pipelines, and ordered transports. Naming the queue is essential: an HTTP response-order dependency is not the same mechanism as a missing TCP byte. Removing one ordered queue can leave other shared limits and dependencies intact.

head-of-line-blocking.title: HTTP/1.1 pipelining and response order
head-of-line-blocking.body: With HTTP/1.1 pipelining, a client can submit multiple requests before earlier responses finish, but responses on that connection retain ordering requirements. A slow first response can delay later results. Opening additional connections can reduce that particular dependency while adding setup and resource costs. Ordinary sequential use and pipelining are different cases; neither should be described as HTTP/2-style interleaving of independent framed response streams.

head-of-line-blocking.title: HTTP/2 multiplexing still rides TCP ordering
head-of-line-blocking.body: HTTP/2 can interleave frames for several streams, allowing useful application-level scheduling. However, TCP delivers one ordered byte stream to the HTTP/2 implementation. If bytes are missing, later received TCP bytes may wait for recovery even when they contain frames for another HTTP stream. Thus multiplexing removes one kind of serialization without removing cross-stream loss blocking imposed by the underlying transport.

head-of-line-blocking.title: QUIC reduces one dependency, not every wait
head-of-line-blocking.body: QUIC provides separate ordered streams, so missing data on one stream need not block available data on another stream in the same way as a shared TCP byte stream. Streams still compete for congestion-controlled path capacity and connection resources, and application dependencies remain. A stylesheet needed before rendering cannot be skipped merely because its transport stream is independent. Diagnose the actual dependency before promising a protocol upgrade eliminates delay.

udp-internals.title: The eight-byte header
udp-internals.body: UDP's base header contains source port, destination port, length, and checksum, each two bytes. Length includes the UDP header and its payload. The checksum uses relevant IP pseudo-header information as well as UDP data; its requirements differ between IPv4 and IPv6 contexts. This compact format omits TCP's sequence, acknowledgment, and window fields. Smaller headers do not supply integrity against malicious modification or any application-level delivery guarantee.

udp-internals.title: Datagram size and fragmentation
udp-internals.body: A large UDP message can exceed the path's packet size constraints. Fragmentation, where applicable, creates several pieces whose loss can prevent delivery of the original datagram. Reassembly consumes receiver resources and can be affected by middleboxes. Prefer payload sizes and application designs that account for the actual path rather than choosing the largest size accepted by a local API. Tunnels reduce the available inner-packet budget further.

udp-internals.title: Receive queues, truncation, and drops
udp-internals.body: UDP datagrams can be discarded before the application reads them if kernel queues fill. An undersized application receive buffer can truncate a datagram under the API's contract; unread trailing bytes do not become an ordinary continuation of the same datagram on the next read. Inspect receive flags, counters, and buffer sizing. A low CPU reading alone does not prove a receiver is keeping up with bursty traffic.

udp-internals.title: Building safe request correlation
udp-internals.body: Include an application identifier when multiple requests can be outstanding and validate the response's source and structure. Retries require duplicate handling because the first request might have succeeded while its response was lost. Add deadlines and congestion-aware rate control as needed. Do not assume a UDP connect operation proves a peer accepted anything: it can merely configure local endpoint behavior without an on-wire establishment exchange.

tcp-tuning-knobs.title: Socket buffers and effective windows
tcp-tuning-knobs.body: Receive and send buffer settings influence memory available to the transport, but the usable receive window, congestion window, and application queue are different measurements. Automatic tuning and platform accounting complicate direct comparisons with configured numbers. Begin with bandwidth-delay product and observed window limits. Raising a buffer limit is justified only when that mechanism constrains the workload; otherwise it can increase memory consumption or hide excessive queueing.

tcp-tuning-knobs.title: Nagle, delayed acknowledgments, and small writes
tcp-tuning-knobs.body: Nagle-related coalescing can reduce inefficient small transmissions, while delayed acknowledgment behavior reduces acknowledgment overhead under its own rules. Certain request patterns can expose interactions that increase latency. TCP_NODELAY disables Nagle's algorithm for the socket but does not disable every source of delay. First combine logically adjacent writes where appropriate, then test latency and packet overhead with the actual application pattern and network conditions.

tcp-tuning-knobs.title: Keepalive, application heartbeat, and timeout
tcp-tuning-knobs.body: TCP keepalive can help detect some idle broken connections when enabled and configured, but default timing may not match an application's deadline. An application heartbeat can test a stronger service-level path, while an operation timeout bounds one request's waiting. These mechanisms answer different questions. Keepalive success cannot prove a remote handler is responsive or that a transaction completed, and aggressive probes multiply load across many idle connections.

tcp-tuning-knobs.title: Backlogs, ephemeral ports, and a tuning experiment
tcp-tuning-knobs.body: Listener queues, accepted-socket handling, ephemeral-port availability, and TIME-WAIT behavior influence connection churn. Increasing a backlog does not create workers able to process requests. Change one relevant setting under a controlled workload, record throughput, error rate, p95/p99 latency, queue length, CPU, and memory, and compare with the baseline. Preserve the configuration and measurement interval so a later result can distinguish a real improvement from cache warming or traffic variation.

dns-hierarchy.title: Names, labels, and delegated zones
dns-hierarchy.body: A domain name is a sequence of labels in a hierarchical namespace. The root sits above top-level domains, and authority can be delegated further down. A zone is the portion administered under a particular authority; it is not always identical to every descendant of a domain name because subdomains can be delegated elsewhere. Distinguish naming hierarchy from server placement: one provider can host many unrelated zones on shared infrastructure.

dns-hierarchy.title: Root, TLD, and authoritative roles
dns-hierarchy.body: A root server can direct a resolver toward servers for a top-level domain. Those servers can direct it toward the relevant delegated zone. The zone's authoritative servers provide its records or appropriate negative answers. Root servers do not contain a complete table of every website's IP address. Cached delegations often avoid repeating the upper steps, so a normal lookup need not contact a root server each time.

dns-hierarchy.title: Delegation glue and circular dependencies
dns-hierarchy.body: A delegation names authoritative servers. If a server's name lies inside the delegated namespace, a resolver may need address information to reach it before it can ask that server for addresses. Relevant glue records supplied with delegations help break this circular dependency. Glue is not a substitute for maintaining correct authoritative address data. Changes to nameserver identity can therefore require coordinated updates in more than one administrative location.

dns-hierarchy.title: Administrative debugging example
dns-hierarchy.body: A team edits an A record in a provider dashboard but the parent still delegates the zone to a different provider. The new record is internally consistent yet invisible to ordinary public resolution. Check the registrar's delegation, the actual authoritative servers, and their answers separately. Then inspect cached delegation lifetimes. A correct endpoint IP in one control panel does not prove the global naming path reaches that record.

recursive-vs-iterative.title: Stub request and recursive service
recursive-vs-iterative.body: A stub resolver on a host normally asks a configured recursive service to obtain an answer. The recursive service performs the required work or returns a failure under its policy. The host might communicate first with a local caching stub, which forwards onward. This layered arrangement means the resolver shown in an application configuration is not necessarily the only cache or upstream participant involved in resolution.

recursive-vs-iterative.title: Iterative referrals and cache reuse
recursive-vs-iterative.body: In an iterative resolution path, a queried server can return a referral toward servers closer to the requested authority. The resolver follows those referrals and assembles an answer, reusing cached records and delegation information when permitted. It need not start at the root if it already knows a suitable delegation. A diagram showing three queries is an example of one cold path, not a fixed number of packets for all names.

recursive-vs-iterative.title: Forwarding changes who performs the work
recursive-vs-iterative.body: A recursive service can forward questions to another resolver rather than contacting authorities itself. Enterprise networks may forward selected suffixes internally and public names elsewhere, producing split resolution behavior. A forwarding loop can cause timeouts despite each individual server being reachable. Draw the configured chain and verify suffix policy, recursion permissions, and upstream addresses before interpreting a single dig result as the entire DNS system.

recursive-vs-iterative.title: Referral, negative answer, and failure differ
recursive-vs-iterative.body: A referral tells the resolver where to continue; NXDOMAIN reports that the queried name does not exist under the applicable answer; an empty successful answer can mean the name exists without the requested record type. SERVFAIL and timeout represent other failures. These outcomes need different recovery. Retrying a deliberate negative answer continuously cannot repair a misspelled name, while an unreachable upstream can require path or configuration investigation.

dns-record-types.title: A, AAAA, CNAME, and PTR
dns-record-types.body: A records map names to IPv4 addresses and AAAA records to IPv6 addresses. A CNAME identifies an alias target and has coexistence restrictions at its owner name. PTR records are used for reverse naming, often under address-derived reverse zones. Forward and reverse records are maintained separately, so matching them is not automatic. A DNS alias also does not change the browser's URL path, certificate requirements, or requested HTTP authority.

dns-record-types.title: NS, SOA, and MX
dns-record-types.body: NS records identify authoritative nameservers, while SOA records carry zone administration information such as serial and timing-related parameters. MX records identify mail exchangers with preferences; they do not contain mailbox contents or ordinary web redirects. Updating a zone serial is relevant to some transfer and synchronization workflows. Diagnose the particular record's consumers rather than assuming every type ultimately means a browser should connect directly to its value.

dns-record-types.title: TXT, SRV, CAA, and service metadata
dns-record-types.body: TXT records carry strings interpreted by higher-level conventions, including some domain-verification and email-policy uses. SRV records describe service locations with priority, weight, port, and target information. CAA records express certificate-issuance policy. Newer service-binding records support additional endpoint metadata. A resolver returns typed data, but the requesting application must understand its meaning; publishing a record does not automatically make every client support the associated protocol.

dns-record-types.title: Record sets, TTLs, and a migration example
dns-record-types.body: Several records of one type can form a resource record set for a name. Clients and resolvers apply record-specific selection and caching behavior; multiple addresses are not a complete health-aware load balancer. During migration, change the relevant A and AAAA sets consistently and account for cached lifetimes. Check whether aliases, mail records, or service records still lead elsewhere before assuming editing one A record moved every service attached to the domain.

dns-caching-and-ttls.title: Countdown starts with the cached answer
dns-caching-and-ttls.body: A resolver that caches an answer with TTL 300 seconds can generally reuse it during that remaining lifetime under the applicable rules. After 120 seconds, about 180 seconds remain for that cached copy. Changing the authoritative TTL later does not remotely rewrite this history. Different resolvers queried at different times therefore expire their copies at different moments, even when all follow the same original record policy.

dns-caching-and-ttls.title: Negative caching has operational effects
dns-caching-and-ttls.body: The absence of a name or a requested record can also be cached under DNS's negative-caching rules. Creating a previously missing record does not necessarily make every client see it immediately. This matters when provisioning a hostname just before issuing a certificate or starting a service. Examine response codes and relevant authority information rather than assuming only positive address answers can explain a stale client observation.

dns-caching-and-ttls.title: Multiple cache layers and stale-answer policies
dns-caching-and-ttls.body: A browser, operating-system stub, local resolver, forwarding service, and recursive resolver can each affect lookup behavior. Implementations may have policies such as prefetching or serving stale data under specified failure conditions. Consequently, observed behavior can differ from a diagram that models a single cache with strict expiry. Record which component supplied an answer and its remaining TTL; flushing one layer does not prove all others are empty.

dns-caching-and-ttls.title: A planned cutover timeline
dns-caching-and-ttls.body: If an old record can remain cached for one hour, lower its TTL more than one old lifetime before a planned switch when possible. Keep the old endpoint serving while old answers drain, then update the authoritative address and observe representative clients. Lower TTLs trade more queries and dependency on resolver availability for quicker normal refresh. They cannot guarantee instant convergence or compensate for an application retaining an address independently.

anycast-and-geodns.title: Anycast selects a routing destination
anycast-and-geodns.body: With anycast, multiple sites advertise reachability to the same service address. Routing policy chooses which site a client reaches, often favoring a topologically convenient path but not necessarily the geographically nearest location. Site advertisements and withdrawal strategy affect failover. A routing change can move packets to another instance, so connection-oriented services must consider state continuity rather than assuming an address uniquely identifies one machine for the session's lifetime.

anycast-and-geodns.title: GeoDNS selects an answer before connection
anycast-and-geodns.body: GeoDNS responds with addresses chosen using available location and policy signals. The visible requester may be a recursive resolver, and extensions or provider policies can alter what client information is available. The chosen answer is then cached. A DNS change therefore influences later resolutions rather than immediately rerouting every existing connection. Traffic steering quality depends on resolver placement, TTLs, health data, and actual application performance.

anycast-and-geodns.title: Health-aware steering and failure boundaries
anycast-and-geodns.body: A service can withdraw an anycast advertisement or stop returning an endpoint in DNS when a site becomes unsuitable. Detection, decision, propagation, cache expiry, and client retry are separate delays. Removing a site too aggressively can overload remaining sites and amplify a partial failure. Define what healthy means for serving requests, including dependencies and capacity, rather than relying only on a successful TCP port probe.

anycast-and-geodns.title: Combining both approaches
anycast-and-geodns.body: A CDN can use DNS to choose a service group and anycast routing to select a location within that group. This combines two decision points with different visibility and timing. To debug a distant edge, record the resolver, returned address, route observation, edge identity, and measured RTT. Changing DNS TTL alone cannot fix an unfavorable route to an unchanged anycast address, and changing BGP policy does not clear a cached DNS selection.

doh-and-dot.title: DoT's dedicated TLS transport
doh-and-dot.body: DNS over TLS protects DNS exchanges over a TLS connection to a resolver, conventionally using a dedicated service port. Establishing the secure connection includes validating the intended resolver according to client policy. Encryption hides query content from straightforward observers of that segment, but the selected resolver still sees the queries it processes. A blocked or intercepted transport path is distinct from an authoritative DNS failure.

doh-and-dot.title: DoH uses HTTP semantics for DNS messages
doh-and-dot.body: DNS over HTTPS carries DNS exchanges inside HTTPS requests and responses. It can use existing HTTP infrastructure and connection management, while adding relevant HTTP behavior to the resolution path. The configured resolver endpoint and bootstrap mechanism matter: resolving the resolver's own hostname can create an initial dependency. Browser-level DoH can also use a different resolver path from ordinary operating-system tools, explaining apparently inconsistent results.

doh-and-dot.title: Encryption, authenticity, and privacy boundaries
doh-and-dot.body: Encrypted transport authenticates the resolver endpoint under the secure-channel policy and protects traffic on that hop. DNSSEC separately validates signed DNS data through its trust chain. Neither alone prevents a chosen resolver from observing requested names, and destination traffic still exposes other metadata. State the threat model explicitly: local-network confidentiality, authoritative answer integrity, and minimizing resolver knowledge are different goals with different mechanisms.

doh-and-dot.title: Fallback and split-horizon behavior
doh-and-dot.body: An enterprise may resolve internal names only through an internal resolver. Sending those questions to a public encrypted resolver can produce failures or leak naming information. Clients also differ in whether transport failure triggers fallback to another resolver or unencrypted DNS. Test normal, unavailable-resolver, and internal-domain cases. A secure-looking settings toggle is incomplete evidence unless actual resolver selection and fallback behavior match the intended policy.

dnssec.title: Signed record sets and verification keys
dnssec.body: DNSSEC signs resource record sets rather than encrypting individual queries. RRSIG records carry signatures, and DNSKEY records supply zone keys used in validation. A validating resolver checks that the data is covered by an acceptable signature and key under the trust model. The signatures do not assert that a website is benign; they establish data authenticity relative to the signed zone and its valid delegation chain.

dnssec.title: DS records connect parent and child trust
dnssec.body: A parent can publish a DS record that identifies a child-zone key, linking validation from a trusted parent toward the child's DNSKEY information. A configured trust anchor starts the validation chain. Missing or inconsistent DS and key information can break an otherwise reachable zone. Key rollovers require coordination and overlap that accounts for caches; replacing one key file does not instantly update every validating resolver's view.

dnssec.title: Authenticated denial of existence
dnssec.body: A resolver needs evidence for negative answers as well as positive ones; otherwise an attacker could falsely claim a signed name was absent. DNSSEC uses mechanisms such as NSEC or NSEC3 to support authenticated denial under their rules. NXDOMAIN, insecure unsigned data, and bogus validation are different outcomes. Do not report a validation failure as an ordinary absent name or silently treat invalid signed data as authenticated.

dnssec.title: Operational diagnosis and response size
dnssec.body: Signatures and supporting records make DNS responses larger and can expose path, truncation, or transport-fallback problems. Time validity also depends on an appropriate clock. When validation fails, inspect the authoritative data, parent delegation, signatures, keys, timestamps, and actual resolver status. Disabling validation may make an answer appear but removes the property being tested; it does not repair the underlying chain or establish that the result is trustworthy.

debugging-dns.title: Start with the exact question and resolver
debugging-dns.body: Record the fully qualified name, record type, resolver address, network context, and timestamp. A command such as dig example.com A asks a different question from dig example.com AAAA, and a short hostname may be expanded through search suffixes. Compare the resolver actually used by the failing application with the one used by a terminal. Browser caches, local hosts files, VPN DNS policy, and encrypted resolvers can produce legitimate differences.

debugging-dns.title: Read response codes and sections
debugging-dns.body: Inspect status, answer, authority, additional information, and remaining TTL instead of copying only the first address. NXDOMAIN indicates the name does not exist in the response's view; NOERROR with no requested answer can indicate absent type data; SERVFAIL indicates failure to obtain an acceptable result. A timeout supplies no equivalent naming conclusion. These distinctions separate misspellings, delegation failures, validation problems, and unreachable resolvers.

debugging-dns.title: Compare recursive and authoritative observations
debugging-dns.body: A query directed to a selected resolver, such as dig @192.0.2.53 example.com A in a documentation example, isolates that service's view.
