After identifying real authoritative servers, compare their answers and delegation information. Trace-style resolution can help locate referrals, but its path can differ from the application's configured forwarding chain. Never substitute a public trace for testing internal split-horizon or access-controlled naming behavior.

debugging-dns.title: Build a reproducible stale-record report
debugging-dns.body: Capture the old and new answers with timestamps, TTLs, server identities, and record types. Check all authoritative instances for consistency and confirm that the parent delegates to the intended provider. If only one recursive resolver is stale within the old TTL, that may be normal caching. If one authoritative server disagrees indefinitely, investigate publication or synchronization. Repeatedly flushing a client cache cannot repair inconsistent authoritative data.

http-request-response-anatomy.title: Request line, authority, fields, and content
http-request-response-anatomy.body: In HTTP/1.1, an ordinary origin request begins with a line such as GET /items/7 HTTP/1.1, followed by fields including Host and a blank line before any message content. The target can include a query string, while a URL fragment remains client-side. Fields describe authentication, representation preferences, and other metadata. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 encode corresponding semantics with framed messages and pseudo-fields rather than the same textual request line.

http-request-response-anatomy.title: Response status and representation metadata
http-request-response-anatomy.body: An HTTP response communicates status, fields, and possibly content. A successful JSON response may use 200 with Content-Type: application/json; a successful operation can also return another appropriate status without a representation. Content-Type describes how bytes should be interpreted, while Content-Encoding describes a content coding such as compression. Neither guarantees that the body is well formed. Validate the documented response contract separately from receiving a syntactically valid HTTP message.

http-request-response-anatomy.title: Message framing and connection reuse
http-request-response-anatomy.body: HTTP/1.1 determines message boundaries through rules involving methods, statuses, transfer coding, content length, and connection closure. A parser must apply the protocol's precedence and rejection rules, not guess from a TCP read boundary. Conflicting Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding handling across intermediaries can create request desynchronization. Reusing a connection safely depends on every participant agreeing where one message ends and the next begins.

http-request-response-anatomy.title: An end-to-end request exercise
http-request-response-anatomy.body: Send a small request to a local test service and record method, target, authority, status, media type, declared length or framing, and observed body. Then return the same application result through a reverse proxy and compare fields and connection boundaries. The proxy may terminate one connection and establish another while preserving HTTP meaning. A browser waterfall therefore cannot be assumed to show the origin server's exact TCP exchange.

http-methods-and-idempotency.title: GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS
http-methods-and-idempotency.body: GET requests a selected representation; HEAD requests corresponding metadata without response content; OPTIONS asks about communication options for a target. These methods have safe semantics, although incidental logging or accounting can still occur. Safe means the client is not requesting the unsafe state change. A crawler, prefetcher, or retrying client may issue retrieval requests automatically, so using GET to purchase an item creates behavior inconsistent with those assumptions.

http-methods-and-idempotency.title: POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE
http-methods-and-idempotency.body: POST asks the target to process submitted content according to resource-specific semantics. PUT requests creation or replacement of the target's state with the supplied representation. PATCH applies a specified partial modification and is not automatically idempotent. DELETE requests removal of the target's association under the service's semantics. PUT and DELETE are idempotent by intended effect, but repeated requests can legitimately receive different statuses or response bodies.

http-methods-and-idempotency.title: CONNECT, TRACE, and intermediary concerns
http-methods-and-idempotency.body: CONNECT requests a tunnel to the identified destination, commonly through a proxy. TRACE is a diagnostic loopback method with security and deployment considerations; many services disable it. Method support must match the resource and policy rather than assuming every endpoint implements every standardized method. Proxies and browsers may impose additional constraints. A 405 response signals a method problem at the target, distinct from authentication failure or an unavailable network path.

http-methods-and-idempotency.title: Conditional requests and retry-safe updates
http-methods-and-idempotency.body: Two clients can overwrite each other's changes even when both use idempotent PUT. A validator and If-Match condition can make an update depend on the version the client actually read, avoiding an unchecked lost update. For a POST payment, a durable idempotency key can distinguish retrying the same operation from creating a new one. Idempotency, concurrency control, and authentication solve separate correctness problems and often must be combined.

status-codes.title: Informational and successful outcomes
status-codes.body: The 1xx class provides interim information; 100 Continue supports a body-send decision, while 101 has protocol-switching semantics in applicable versions. A 200 response indicates success with method-specific meaning, 201 indicates creation, 202 indicates acceptance without promising completion, and 204 has no response content. An asynchronous job accepted with 202 still needs a result-retrieval contract. Do not tell a user their operation completed solely because its submission was accepted.

status-codes.title: Redirection and cached representations
status-codes.body: 301 and 308 express permanent redirection, while 302 and 307 express temporary redirection; method handling differs, with 307 and 308 preserving the method under their semantics. A 303 directs retrieval of another resource. A 304 is used with conditional retrieval to permit reuse of a stored representation rather than behaving like an ordinary redirect to a new page. Clients should apply redirect limits and handle credentials across changed origins deliberately.

status-codes.title: Client errors need specific recovery
status-codes.body: 400 indicates a request problem; 401 concerns authentication and its challenge; 403 means refusal under policy; 404 indicates no available target representation in the response's semantics; 405 concerns an unsupported method. 409 can express conflict, 412 a failed precondition, 413 an oversized request, and 429 rate limiting. These are not interchangeable retry signals. Fixing the request, renewing authentication, waiting, or resolving a version conflict require different client actions.

status-codes.title: Server errors and ambiguous side effects
status-codes.body: 500 indicates an internal failure, 502 an invalid upstream response at a gateway, 503 temporary unavailability, and 504 an upstream timeout at a gateway. None alone guarantees that every downstream side effect was rolled back. A gateway can time out after an origin commits. Retry only under the operation's safety contract and remaining deadline, and record the responding hop so a proxy's status is not automatically attributed to the final application.

http-headers.title: Representation and negotiation fields
http-headers.body: Content-Type identifies the media type, Content-Encoding identifies applied content coding, and Content-Length participates in applicable size or framing semantics. Accept and Accept-Encoding describe client preferences and capabilities. Vary tells caches which request fields affected representation selection. A server returning gzip content should not send that representation to an incompatible client merely because the URL is the same. Treat metadata and cache selection as one coherent representation contract.

http-headers.title: Caching validators and freshness directives
http-headers.body: Cache-Control expresses storage and reuse policy, while ETag and Last-Modified can support validation. If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since make suitable requests conditional. An ETag is an opaque validator rather than a value a client should parse as a timestamp or file hash. Strong and weak validation have different uses. Correct caching depends on both freshness policy and variant identity, especially for personalized or negotiated responses.

http-headers.title: Authentication, cookies, and forwarded identity
http-headers.body: Authorization carries authentication credentials under a scheme; Cookie returns client-held cookie state, while Set-Cookie has special response semantics and cannot be combined blindly like a generic comma-separated field. Forwarded and similar proxy fields are assertions from the sender unless a trusted boundary sanitizes them. An application should accept client identity metadata only through its configured trusted proxy chain, with direct bypass paths accounted for.

http-headers.title: Hop-specific behavior and parsing rules
http-headers.body: Some fields describe one connection or intermediary hop rather than end-to-end representation meaning. HTTP versions impose different restrictions on connection-specific fields. Header names are case-insensitive, but values follow their own grammars; duplicates and whitespace cannot all be normalized by one arbitrary rule. When debugging, compare ingress and egress metadata at each proxy and use maintained parsers to avoid disagreements about authentication, framing, or cache keys.

http-1-vs-2-vs-3.title: HTTP/1.1: ordered messages and connection management
http-1-vs-2-vs-3.body: HTTP/1.1 commonly uses persistent TCP connections carrying textual field syntax and defined message framing. Clients can use several connections for concurrency, while pipelined responses on one connection retain ordering constraints. Setup cost, idle connection policy, and message boundaries therefore strongly affect performance. HTTP/1.1 does not imply one connection per request, and connection reuse does not remove application dependencies between sequential requests.

http-1-vs-2-vs-3.title: HTTP/2: frames, streams, and HPACK
http-1-vs-2-vs-3.body: HTTP/2 maps exchanges onto streams within one connection and interleaves frames, reducing dependence on multiple parallel connections for application concurrency. It uses HPACK field compression and stream plus connection flow control. TCP underneath still provides one ordered byte stream, so packet loss can delay delivery across HTTP streams. Stream concurrency and prioritization also depend on endpoint behavior; multiplexing does not create unlimited server execution capacity.

http-1-vs-2-vs-3.title: HTTP/3: HTTP over QUIC
http-1-vs-2-vs-3.body: HTTP/3 uses QUIC streams, integrated secure transport establishment, and QPACK field compression. Independent stream delivery changes how loss affects unrelated responses, while connection identifiers can support suitable path changes. QUIC itself runs over UDP but implements congestion control and reliable stream mechanisms. Networks that block or degrade the relevant UDP path can require another negotiated protocol. Verify actual usage instead of assuming the newest browser always connects with HTTP/3.

http-1-vs-2-vs-3.title: A fair comparison experiment
http-1-vs-2-vs-3.body: Compare the same content, server work, client location, cache state, and reuse state across versions. Test cold setup, warm reuse, loss, and multiple concurrent resources separately. Measure useful completion time and tail latency, not merely protocol labels. A slow database remains slow under every HTTP version; a lossy multiplexed download may show a different result. Report negotiated versions at each proxy hop because browser-to-edge and edge-to-origin protocols can differ.

persistent-connections.title: Reuse amortizes connection establishment
persistent-connections.body: A reusable connection avoids repeating some transport and security setup for every request. For short requests over a long-RTT path, saved round trips can dominate payload transfer time. Reuse requires correct message framing and lifecycle management so completed response data is not mistaken for the next exchange. A persistent connection is a resource with idle and total lifetime policies, not a guarantee that a peer or intermediary will keep it indefinitely.

persistent-connections.title: Sequential reuse, pipelining, and multiplexing
persistent-connections.body: Sequential reuse waits for one exchange before starting another on the connection. Pipelining submits several requests without waiting for preceding responses but preserves applicable response order. Multiplexing interleaves distinguishable streams, as in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. These choices have different dependency behavior. Calling all three keep-alive hides why a slow response can block another request in one configuration while independent streams progress in another.

persistent-connections.title: Pool size and application concurrency
persistent-connections.body: A pool bounds connections and decides which requests wait for one. With HTTP/1.1, too few active connections can serialize independent work; too many can overload the service. Multiplexed protocols add stream limits within each connection, so a connection count alone no longer describes concurrency. Include waiting time for a pool slot in request deadlines. Otherwise a nominal 500 ms network timeout can hide seconds spent waiting before the connection is acquired.

persistent-connections.title: Stale connections and safe retry
persistent-connections.body: An idle connection may be closed by the server, a proxy, or an intervening stateful device. A client can discover this during reuse, possibly after some bytes were transmitted. Discard the unusable connection and apply the operation's retry policy, preserving its identity and deadline. Automatically replaying every request on a new connection can duplicate side effects. Track connection age, idle duration, reuse failures, and upstream policy to select sensible pool lifetimes.

http-2-internals.title: Frame types and stream identifiers
http-2-internals.body: HTTP/2 frames carry a length, type, flags, and stream association where applicable. HEADERS describe message metadata, DATA carries content, SETTINGS exchanges connection parameters, WINDOW_UPDATE grants flow-control credit, RST_STREAM terminates a stream, and GOAWAY signals connection shutdown boundaries. Some frames act on the connection rather than one request. Knowing the frame type explains whether an observation affects a single exchange or every stream sharing the transport.

http-2-internals.title: Stream lifecycle and multiplexed exchanges
http-2-internals.body: A stream can move through states such as idle, open, half-closed, and closed under protocol rules. Finishing the request direction does not necessarily mean the response is complete. Stream identifiers allow interleaved frames to be associated correctly, but the application must still bound concurrent work and retained data. A cancelled user request may require both protocol signaling and cancellation of backend processing; closing a stream does not automatically undo a committed operation.

http-2-internals.title: HPACK field compression state
http-2-internals.body: HPACK compresses field blocks using defined representations and tables, allowing repeated metadata to be encoded efficiently. Dynamic compression state belongs to the connection, so decoding depends on the correct sequence and state. Compression reduces overhead but provides no confidentiality; secure deployments rely on appropriate transport security. Large or malicious field blocks still need limits and robust parsing, and compressed size alone is insufficient to bound decoded memory use.

http-2-internals.title: Two flow-control budgets and shutdown
http-2-internals.body: DATA transmission is constrained by both stream and connection credit. A stream with available credit can still wait if the shared connection window is exhausted. Applications should consume or cancel unwanted data deliberately so shared resources do not stall. GOAWAY helps peers understand which streams may have been processed during shutdown, but retry decisions still need request semantics. TCP loss and congestion remain separate constraints below HTTP/2's flow-control mechanism.

http-3-and-quic.title: QUIC packets and reliable streams
http-3-and-quic.body: QUIC carries protocol packets in UDP datagrams and implements its own acknowledgment, loss recovery, congestion control, and stream delivery. Stream offsets identify data independently from packet numbers, allowing retransmitted information to be carried in new packets rather than treating the packet itself as the application object. HTTP/3 maps requests and responses onto these streams. Saying UDP is unreliable therefore does not describe the guarantees supplied by the full QUIC transport.

http-3-and-quic.title: TLS integration and connection establishment
http-3-and-quic.body: QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 handshake functions into its transport rather than wrapping an already established TCP stream. Connection establishment derives protection keys and negotiates parameters under QUIC's rules. Resumption and permitted early data can reduce startup delay, but early actions remain replay-sensitive. Applications cannot infer that a payment is safe to repeat merely because its first bytes were encrypted and sent before normal handshake completion.

http-3-and-quic.title: Connection IDs, migration, and path validation
http-3-and-quic.body: A connection identifier helps distinguish a QUIC connection from only its current IP-address and port tuple. This supports continuity through suitable address changes, such as switching access networks, subject to peer support and path validation. Validation tests reachability on the new path and helps limit misuse. The new path can have different MTU, delay, loss, and capacity, so preserving connection identity does not preserve the old path's performance characteristics.

http-3-and-quic.title: QPACK and remaining blocking constraints
http-3-and-quic.body: HTTP/3 uses QPACK for field compression with mechanisms designed around QUIC stream behavior. Compression dependencies can still require bounded waiting under protocol rules. Individual streams remain ordered, connection-level resource limits are shared, and congestion affects the whole path. Thus HTTP/3 removes particular cross-stream TCP dependencies rather than all blocking. Compare application dependency graphs and flow-control state before attributing every delay to packet loss.

tls-handshake.title: ClientHello and ServerHello choose the context
tls-handshake.body: In a typical certificate-authenticated TLS 1.3 handshake, ClientHello offers supported versions, algorithms, extensions, and key-share information. ServerHello selects compatible parameters and provides its corresponding key-share information. The peers derive handshake protection from the negotiated exchange. A HelloRetryRequest can add an extra exchange when needed. This sequence establishes cryptographic context, but the client still needs to validate the server identity before trusting the resulting application channel.

tls-handshake.title: Server authentication messages
tls-handshake.body: After ServerHello, the server sends protected handshake information including EncryptedExtensions and, in the ordinary certificate mode, Certificate and CertificateVerify, followed by Finished. CertificateVerify proves possession of the relevant private key through a signature bound to the handshake context. Finished authenticates the transcript under derived keys. Certificate parsing alone is insufficient: the client must validate the chain, intended hostname, validity, and policy as well as the proof and transcript.

tls-handshake.title: Client Finished and application traffic
tls-handshake.body: The client verifies the server's messages and sends its Finished to confirm the handshake transcript and key derivation. Optional client authentication adds its own messages and validation requirements. Application traffic uses derived traffic keys with direction-specific protection. This is different from using the server certificate's public key to encrypt every HTTP byte. Modern handshakes use asymmetric mechanisms for authentication or key agreement and symmetric authenticated encryption for bulk traffic.

tls-handshake.title: Resumption, early data, and deployment failures
tls-handshake.body: Resumption uses previously established material to reduce later handshake work under the selected mode. Optional early data permits selected application bytes before ordinary completion but has replay considerations, so unsuitable side effects must not be accepted blindly. Common failures include incompatible parameters, missing intermediates, an incorrect hostname, expired credentials, and clock problems. Record the actual failing handshake stage; a generic TLS error does not prove packet routing is broken.

certificates-and-pki.title: Leaf identity and proof of private-key possession
certificates-and-pki.body: A leaf certificate contains a subject public key, validity interval, issuer information, identity names, and constraints under a signature. The certificate can be public; the private key is what enables the server's proof of possession. A copied certificate without its corresponding private key does not suffice for the normal authenticated handshake. Conversely, a stolen private key can be serious even though no certificate file was hidden in the first place.

certificates-and-pki.title: Trust paths, intermediates, and roots
certificates-and-pki.body: A client builds an acceptable chain from the leaf through issuing intermediates toward a trusted anchor in its configured trust store. Trust is local to that client environment; different systems can have different anchors and policies. Servers commonly need to supply appropriate intermediates rather than assuming every client has cached them. A root certificate being self-signed is not what grants trust—the client's explicit trust configuration provides that starting authority.

certificates-and-pki.title: Names, constraints, and lifecycle
certificates-and-pki.body: Validation checks the requested service identity and applicable certificate constraints, not simply whether any signature verifies. The subject alternative names, validity period, key usage, extended usage, and policy can affect acceptance. Issuance, renewal, deployment, and revocation handling are separate lifecycle steps. Renewing a certificate in a control plane does not prove every edge and origin instance now serves it or that each private key is protected appropriately.

certificates-and-pki.title: A multi-endpoint validation exercise
certificates-and-pki.body: Test the intended hostname against each relevant serving endpoint while preserving name indication and hostname verification. Compare the presented leaf, intermediates, dates, and chain result. A subset of failing clients may expose a missing intermediate, stale instance, different trust store, or clock issue. Disabling validation hides these differences and removes peer authentication; it cannot establish that the deployment is correct or the remote endpoint is the intended service.

http-caching.title: Storage permission and freshness lifetime
http-caching.body: A cache first determines whether a response can be stored, then whether it is fresh enough for reuse. Cache-Control directives such as max-age and s-maxage express relevant freshness policy, while private restricts shared-cache storage and no-store prohibits storage under the directive's rules. no-cache allows storage but requires validation before reuse. Distinguishing storage from reuse prevents the common mistake of treating no-cache as an instruction to erase every copy.

http-caching.title: Validators and conditional retrieval
http-caching.body: A stored response can retain an ETag or Last-Modified value. A later request using If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since can ask whether the representation changed. A suitable 304 response allows reuse of the stored body with updated metadata under the rules. This saves body transfer but still pays a validation exchange. A genuinely fresh cached response can avoid that exchange entirely, which is a different latency benefit.

http-caching.title: Cache keys and representation variants
http-caching.body: The selected representation can depend on more than the URL, including fields identified by Vary and service-specific cache policy. Compressed and uncompressed representations, language variants, or authenticated content must not be mixed accidentally. Shared caches need deliberate handling for credentials and personalized responses. A high hit ratio is not success if users receive incompatible or private data; verify the identity and permitted audience of every reusable representation.

http-caching.title: Invalidation and a concrete policy choice
http-caching.body: An immutable fingerprinted asset can use a long freshness lifetime because a changed file receives a new URL. A mutable HTML document often needs shorter freshness or validation so it references current assets. An account response may require restrictive storage policy. Purging one CDN does not erase browser caches or other intermediaries. Design URLs, freshness, validators, and rollback behavior together instead of relying on a universal cache-busting switch.

websockets.title: Establishment and message framing
websockets.body: A WebSocket connection begins through the establishment mechanism appropriate to its HTTP transport, commonly the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade handshake. After establishment, WebSocket frames carry messages with their own framing rather than ordinary request-response exchanges. Text and binary messages, fragmentation, and control frames have distinct rules. The application still needs a message schema and size limits; a persistent byte path does not automatically define how game actions or chat updates should be interpreted.

websockets.title: Ping, pong, close, and idle paths
websockets.body: Ping and pong control frames support connection liveness mechanisms, while close frames coordinate protocol shutdown with a code and optional reason. Application heartbeats can test additional service-level behavior beyond frame exchange. Proxies and load balancers can impose idle limits even when endpoints would otherwise retain the connection. Choose heartbeat intervals and timeouts based on those boundaries and resource costs, and distinguish orderly close from abrupt transport loss.

websockets.title: Backpressure and bounded outgoing queues
websockets.body: A server broadcasting to many clients must handle a client that stops reading. If each update is appended indefinitely, one slow subscriber can consume unbounded memory. Bound pending bytes or messages and choose an explicit policy: disconnect, coalesce replaceable state, or retain only an allowed history. Dropping an intermediate telemetry sample can be valid, while dropping a financial event silently is not. The policy follows application semantics, not WebSocket framing.

websockets.title: Reconnect, authentication, and replay
websockets.body: A reconnected transport is a new communication context unless the application restores its logical session. Use authenticated session state, stable message identifiers, and a resumable history position where appropriate. Handle credential expiry and permission changes during long connections. If a message was processed before the connection broke but its acknowledgment was lost, the client must avoid inventing a new operation identity on retry. Reconnection alone cannot guarantee exactly-once application effects.

server-sent-events.title: Event-stream format and dispatch
server-sent-events.body: SSE sends an HTTP response using the text/event-stream media type. Fields such as data, event, id, and retry have defined meanings, and a blank line terminates an event for dispatch. Multiple data lines contribute to one event's data. Sending partial text without the required event boundary can leave the browser waiting even though bytes arrived. Correct formatting is therefore part of latency, not merely a cosmetic serialization choice.

server-sent-events.title: Reconnection and Last-Event-ID
server-sent-events.body: An event ID can let a reconnecting client report its last received position through the EventSource mechanism. The server must retain or reconstruct suitable history to resume; assigning IDs alone does not provide storage. Define what happens when the requested position is too old, unknown, or belongs to another stream. The client may need a snapshot followed by new events instead of replaying an unlimited backlog.

server-sent-events.title: Proxy buffering, idle timeouts, and heartbeats
server-sent-events.body: A proxy can buffer response bytes rather than forwarding every event promptly. Idle connection policies can also close a healthy but quiet stream. Configure the actual serving chain for streaming and use appropriate periodic comments or activity when required. Verify arrival timestamps at the browser under low event volume. A server log showing immediate writes does not prove intermediaries delivered those bytes to the client immediately.

server-sent-events.title: When one-way streaming is enough
server-sent-events.body: SSE fits server-to-client progress, notifications, and feeds, while user actions can use separate authenticated HTTP requests. It does not provide a general bidirectional message channel on the same stream. Bound subscriber queues and handle slow clients just as with other long-lived transports. For a deployment-progress page, define event ordering, reconnection history, and final completion state so a lost last event does not leave the interface waiting forever.

long-polling-vs-sse-vs-websockets.title: Long polling: one outstanding wait at a time
long-polling-vs-sse-vs-websockets.body: A long-poll request waits until an event is available or a bounded timeout occurs, after which the client issues another request. It uses ordinary HTTP infrastructure but repeats request metadata and can leave small gaps between polls. Include a cursor or event identifier so events arriving during reconnect are not lost. Server capacity depends on the implementation's handling of waiting requests, not simply the number of HTTP requests completed per second.

long-polling-vs-sse-vs-websockets.title: SSE: continuous server-to-client delivery
long-polling-vs-sse-vs-websockets.body: SSE keeps a response open and dispatches framed text events as data arrives. Browser EventSource supplies defined reconnection behavior, and event IDs can support application replay. Client actions usually use other requests. This fits dashboards and progress feeds where continuous traffic mainly travels toward the client. Check proxy buffering, retention, and authentication requirements; choosing SSE does not eliminate server-side connection and slow-consumer management.

long-polling-vs-sse-vs-websockets.title: WebSockets: independent traffic in both directions
long-polling-vs-sse-vs-websockets.body: WebSockets support messages initiated by either endpoint over a persistent channel. They can suit collaboration, games, and frequent bidirectional updates, but require application-level reconnection, authorization lifecycle, and delivery semantics. Infrastructure must support the established channel and its idle policy. A more flexible transport also exposes more protocol-design choices: message schemas, acknowledgments, resynchronization, ordering, and queue overflow still need explicit answers.

long-polling-vs-sse-vs-websockets.title: A workload-based decision matrix in words
long-polling-vs-sse-vs-websockets.body: For infrequent server updates and strict compatibility constraints, long polling may be adequate. For a mainly one-way live feed with browser support, SSE often simplifies the client. For frequent independent traffic in both directions, WebSockets may reduce repeated exchange overhead. Estimate connection count, update frequency, message size, acceptable delay, replay horizon, and proxy behavior. Test reconnect storms and slow subscribers before making the choice based solely on idle-request overhead.

grpc-and-protobuf.title: Message schemas and compatible evolution
grpc-and-protobuf.body: Protocol Buffers use numbered fields with defined types in a schema. Field numbers identify wire data, so reusing a removed number for a different meaning can break old readers even if source names look sensible. Preserve compatibility through disciplined additions, reserved identifiers, and understood defaults. Binary serialization can reduce size for some data, but performance depends on payload shape and implementation. A schema is an interface contract, not automatic validation of business rules.

grpc-and-protobuf.title: Four RPC communication patterns
grpc-and-protobuf.body: gRPC supports unary calls, server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming. Unary sends one request and receives one response. Server streaming produces multiple responses to one request; client streaming collects multiple request messages; bidirectional streaming permits independent message sequences in both directions. These forms affect memory, cancellation, ordering, and resource lifetime. A streaming API should define what a message acknowledgment means and how partially completed streams recover.

grpc-and-protobuf.title: Status, metadata, deadlines, and cancellation
grpc-and-protobuf.body: gRPC status is distinct from merely observing a successful underlying HTTP connection. Metadata carries call context, while deadlines bound how long work should remain useful. Propagate the remaining budget to downstream calls rather than resetting a full timeout at every hop. Cancellation is a signal whose completion semantics depend on the work involved; a database commit may have happened before it arrives. Treat timeout outcomes as potentially ambiguous when side effects are involved.

grpc-and-protobuf.title: Flow control and retry boundaries
grpc-and-protobuf.body: Streaming calls can produce data faster than a peer consumes it, requiring flow control and bounded application buffers. The transport's capacity does not justify retaining unlimited decoded messages. Retries and hedging need operation-specific policy, especially when a stream or side effect has partially progressed. For a 500 ms deadline with 200 ms already spent upstream, only the remaining budget should constrain downstream work; otherwise the system performs work the caller can no longer use.

graphql-networking.title: One endpoint can represent very different workloads
graphql-networking.body: A GraphQL request describes selected fields and can trigger many resolver operations behind one HTTP exchange. Network request count therefore understates backend work. Nested collections can multiply database queries or downstream calls, creating N+1 behavior and large responses. Bound query complexity, depth, pagination, and execution time as appropriate. Batching data access can reduce repeated calls, but must preserve authorization and request-specific context.

graphql-networking.title: HTTP transport and error interpretation
graphql-networking.body: GraphQL commonly uses HTTP, but application execution errors and partial data can appear inside a syntactically successful HTTP response. Clients must inspect the documented GraphQL result structure rather than treating status 200 as proof that every requested field succeeded. Transport failures remain separate. A gateway timeout can occur after mutations have run, so retry behavior for mutations requires the same careful operation identity and ambiguity handling as other APIs.

graphql-networking.title: Caching query results and entities
graphql-networking.body: Caching can operate at several levels: HTTP responses, persisted query identifiers, resolver data, or normalized client entities. Arbitrary query bodies and user-specific authorization complicate shared caching. A cache key must account for the query, variables, relevant identity, and representation policy. Invalidating one entity may affect many query results. Define consistency expectations explicitly rather than assuming the flexibility of field selection automatically produces efficient or correct caching.

graphql-networking.title: Subscriptions and production measurement
graphql-networking.body: Subscriptions require a continuing delivery mechanism, often a separately defined WebSocket-based protocol or another supported transport. Reconnection and event replay remain application responsibilities. Measure resolver latency, downstream calls, returned bytes, query complexity, and errors alongside HTTP metrics. If one request downloads a megabyte and launches hundreds of backend operations, a low request-per-second figure does not imply the service is lightly loaded.

mqtt.title: Brokered publish and subscribe
mqtt.body: MQTT clients publish messages to topic names and subscribe through a broker using topic filters. The broker routes matching publications, decoupling publishers from direct knowledge of subscribers. Topic hierarchy and wildcard filters influence both delivery and authorization. A topic name is not automatically a queue with exclusive consumption. Define which identities may publish or subscribe to each namespace, especially when device identifiers appear in topics.

mqtt.title: QoS 0, 1, and 2
mqtt.body: QoS 0 provides at-most-once protocol delivery without the acknowledgment exchange of higher levels. QoS 1 provides at-least-once delivery, so duplicates can occur. QoS 2 uses a more involved protocol exchange to provide exactly-once delivery within its specified protocol scope. That scope does not automatically make a downstream database update exactly once across reconnects or bridges. Application operation identifiers and transactional handling may still be necessary.

mqtt.title: Retained messages and session state
mqtt.body: A retained publication lets a broker supply the retained value to relevant new subscribers according to protocol rules. It is not an unlimited event history. Session settings influence whether subscriptions and queued delivery state survive disconnection, and protocol versions expose different controls. Choose whether a device reconnecting after hours needs the latest state, every missed event, or a fresh snapshot; those are different storage and delivery requirements.

mqtt.title: Keepalive, last will, and constrained clients
mqtt.body: Keepalive helps detect a silent connection, and a configured will message can signal an unexpected disconnect under the broker's rules. A will is not proof that a physical device failed; the network or broker path may have failed instead. Constrained devices need bounded queues, backoff, secure credentials, and an explicit offline policy. Test reconnect storms after power restoration so all devices do not simultaneously overwhelm authentication and message delivery.

smtp-ftp-ssh.title: SMTP moves messages between mail participants
smtp-ftp-ssh.body: SMTP is a store-and-forward mail transfer protocol using a command and reply conversation. Envelope sender and recipients guide transport and differ from human-visible message header fields. A receiving server accepting a message does not guarantee final inbox placement or that a person read it. DNS MX records influence delivery routing, while authentication and transport protection depend on the connection role and configuration. Delayed delivery and bounce handling are part of the workflow.

smtp-ftp-ssh.title: FTP separates control and data connections
smtp-ftp-ssh.body: FTP uses a control conversation for commands and separate connections for file data or directory listings. Active and passive modes differ in which side initiates the data connection, which explains many NAT and firewall complications. A successful login on the control channel does not prove a file transfer path is permitted. Traditional unprotected FTP exposes sensitive information; secure alternatives or appropriately protected variants require deliberate protocol selection and compatible infrastructure.

smtp-ftp-ssh.title: SSH authenticates hosts and users
smtp-ftp-ssh.body: SSH establishes a protected channel, authenticates the server host, and supports user authentication before providing sessions or other allowed functions. Host-key checking protects against connecting to an impostor, while user keys or other configured methods establish client authority. Multiplexed channels can carry shell sessions, forwarding, or subsystems within one connection. Accepting an unexpected host-key change without investigation undermines a separate trust boundary from merely protecting the user's private key.

smtp-ftp-ssh.title: SFTP, FTPS, and troubleshooting distinctions
smtp-ftp-ssh.body: SFTP is an SSH subsystem with its own file-transfer protocol; it is not ordinary FTP with a different port. FTPS applies TLS to FTP and retains FTP's connection-model considerations. Diagnose SMTP delivery using queue and recipient status, FTP transfers using control and data paths, and SSH failures using host authentication, user authentication, and session policy. Grouping all three as old TCP protocols loses the distinct mechanisms that explain their failures.
